description_ru: Медина Марракеша: лабиринт улиц, торг на рынках, мятный чай и мальчик-проводник, который знает дорогу куда лучше, чем автор. Ироничный и красочный путевой очерк.
text:
There are two kinds of visitors to the medina of Marrakech: those who admit that they are lost, and those who are lost and do not yet know it. I belonged to the second category for the first forty minutes, an interval during which I strode confidently through a maze of ochre alleys, consulting a map on my telephone that showed me, with maddening serenity, as a small blue dot floating in an empty white space, like a ghost in a snowfield.

The old city is a labyrinth of such thoroughness that it appears to have been designed by an architect with a grudge against the very idea of a straight line. Its walls, built of rammed earth the colour of cinnamon and dusted with the pink of the surrounding plain, were raised in the twelfth century, and they enclose a tangle of lanes that narrow, twist, split, and then end in a blank wall, a staircase, or a donkey. Some of the lanes are so tight that two people carrying shopping must negotiate their passage with the delicacy of diplomats. Motorbikes, ignoring all of this, thread through the crowd at astonishing speed, announcing themselves by a single warning cry, "Balak!", which means, roughly, "mind yourself", and is the only traffic law that anyone obeys.

Into this predicament, on my first morning, stepped a boy of about twelve in a football shirt, who announced that he was a guide, that he was unofficial, and that the street I was seeking was closed. I had learned from several guidebooks that this was a classic opening, and I thanked him with the slightly exaggerated courtesy of a man who has been warned, and kept walking. He kept walking too, a pace behind me, with a patient and faintly amused air, like a sheepdog following a sheep that thinks it is escaping.

After a further quarter of an hour, in which I passed the same fountain three times, I stopped, defeated, and said to the boy, in an unsteady mixture of French and English, that I would like to go to the Jemaa el-Fnaa, the great square at the heart of the city. He nodded as if I had made an unremarkable request, took a decisive turn through a door that I had assumed belonged to a private house, and led me through a corridor, across a courtyard shared by a woman and several chickens, and out into a lane that smelled overwhelmingly of cumin. His name, he said, was Yassine. His fee, he added, was for me to decide, and would I like some orange juice.

The square came at me all at once, like a wave. By day it is a wide, dusty plaza of snake charmers, henna artists, water sellers in absurdly fringed hats, and orange-juice vendors with pyramids of fruit; by evening it is transformed into the largest open-air restaurant on Earth, with scores of stalls under strings of lights, wreathed in smoke and clamour. Storytellers hold circles of listeners in thrall. Drummers, acrobats and musicians compete for attention, and the wail of a reed pipe comes snaking through the din. UNESCO has recognised the square as a masterpiece of intangible heritage, which is a formal way of saying that nobody has ever succeeded in describing it properly.

Above it all, as a sort of fixed point in the confusion, rises the minaret of the Koutoubia mosque, seventy-seven metres of rose-coloured stone, finished in the twelfth century and visible from almost everywhere. Locals will tell you that it is the only reliable compass in Marrakech, and that, being a tower, it has the advantage of not asking for a tip. I took to glancing up at it from every corner, like a nervous sailor consulting a lighthouse, and it never once failed to look exactly as superior as I had hoped.

The souks, to the north, are another order of experience. They are a warren of covered lanes, roofed with slats of wood so that the sun enters in thin gold stripes, and each trade has its own quarter: the dyers, whose skeins of wool hang dripping in blue and saffron; the metalworkers, whose hammers rattle all day on brass; the leather sellers, whose slippers glow in piles of lemon, scarlet and plum. Everything is for sale, and nothing has a price, for the price is a conversation. I wished to buy a modest lantern, and the shopkeeper, a dignified man in a grey robe, began by offering me tea.

This is the first rule of haggling, and the one that guidebooks fail to stress. One does not bargain; one visits. The tea arrives in a little glass, hot, green and thick with mint and sugar, poured from a height so that it froths, and drunk in small, thoughtful sips while the conversation drifts from lanterns to families to the football scores. After a quarter of an hour the shopkeeper named a price that would have bought a small car. I countered with a sum that would have bought a sandwich. He clutched his chest, called on God, and then, with a smile, the real negotiation began. It ended forty minutes later, with a price we both considered an outrage, and a handshake of genuine warmth.

Yassine, who had been waiting outside with a patience I could only admire, inspected the lantern and gave it a nod. "You paid too much," he said, "but not very much too much, which is the correct amount."

In the evening he led me back through the dark lanes to my riad, one of those hidden houses of the old city whose plain, forbidding door opens onto a court of astonishing luxury, with a fountain, orange trees, and a roof terrace from which the muezzin's call rises from a hundred minarets at once. I paid him what seemed to me a generous sum, and he looked at it, and at me, with a weighing frankness.

"Tomorrow," he said, "you will be lost again. Do you want me to come?"

"I think I shall be lost on my own," I said, with a surge of foolish pride.

He shrugged, and was gone, and the next morning I was lost on my own for exactly forty-five minutes. The boy, in his football shirt, was waiting at the end of the street with an expression of unbearable tact.

questions.question: What does the cry 'Balak' mean?
questions.answer: Roughly, 'mind yourself'; a warning from motorbikes.

questions.question: Who is Yassine?
questions.answer: A boy of about twelve who acts as the writer's unofficial guide.

questions.question: What is the first rule of haggling according to the writer?
questions.answer: One does not bargain; one visits, and begins with tea.

questions.question: What happens the next morning?
questions.answer: The writer is lost again, and Yassine waits at the end of the street.
